basic.title: Basic Turn
basic.description: Start from the real opening entry, then finish one hand action and one wheel action.

steps.welcome: Seven Hatreds has three victory paths: control 16 regions at New Year, capture an opponent's capital, or reach 3 prestige first.
steps.handLimit: At the start of every turn, check hand limit first. Ming may keep 15 cards; Later Jin and the Mongols may keep 10.
steps.openingEntry: After that, look at the live turn entry. This turn still needs two things: one hand action and one wheel action, and the current player decides which comes first.
steps.handResource: Cards are the main resource. Events resolve when played, armaments need one extra discard after being played, tactics stay for battle, and silver cards are pure payment.
steps.selectRegion: Not every action starts with a region pick. Grant Pardon needs a target, so choose Pidao now and you will immediately see control change on the map.
steps.pickAction: Grant Pardon pulls a neighboring enemy troop into Ming control and directly changes ownership on the board.
steps.payCards: Most faction actions require payment before resolution. Discard 3 cards first, then resolve Grant Pardon.
steps.actionResult: The board has already changed. The cards you spent have become real map control.
steps.moraleLevel: The number on top of each troop block is both level and morale. Higher levels roll stronger dice, and a unit only collapses when that level reaches zero.
steps.wheelMove: After the hand action, finish this turn's wheel action. The wheel is what pushes later turns toward diplomacy, attacks, recruitment, Midyear, and New Year.
steps.finish: That is the basic turn structure in Seven Hatreds: convert cards into board pressure, then finish the shared wheel action.

attackAndBattle.title: Attack And Battle
attackAndBattle.description: Enter from a real dispatch target state, then see a live battle settlement and post-battle result.

steps.overview: Attack dispatch is not just choosing one target. Troops have to move into place first, and only then is the battle truly settled.
steps.moveEntry: Start from the live attack dispatch state. The highlighted targets are the real places this force can attack right now.
steps.battleOpen: Once the target is set, read the battle first: how many troops were committed, who is defending, and how wide this battlefield can open.
steps.battleDamage: Battle damage depends on troop type and level. Choose casualty order here, then let the field battle resolve for real.
steps.battleResult: After resolution, read the result first: rolled points, damage dealt, and how many troops survived on each side.
steps.retreatAndDefeat: A battle is not just about winning. Retreat losses, casualty priority, and leftover pressure all matter for what happens next.
steps.finish: A real attack chain means choosing the target, fighting, absorbing losses, reading the outcome, and then deciding how the battle closes.

siege.title: Siege And Occupation
siege.description: See why winning a city battle still leaves a decision between occupation, siege, and withdrawal.

steps.overview: City battles are not the same as field battles. Even after winning, you still decide what state the city enters next.
steps.defendCity: Read the city's current position first. The defenders have been broken, but that does not automatically mean the city has changed hands.
steps.cityBattle: The city-battle result is already here. First read the surviving force and the summary before deciding what happens next.
steps.cityResult: Winning the city fight is not the same as completing occupation. The key question is the state of the city after the battle.
steps.besiegeChoice: Besieging means leaving troops outside to keep pressure on the city. Control does not change yet, but the region enters a siege state.
steps.occupyChoice: Only a true occupation changes control. City warfare is about the post-battle state, not only the fight itself.
steps.finish: The key difference from field battles is that a city battle ends with a state choice: occupation, siege, or stepping back.

diplomacy.title: Diplomacy And Hire
diplomacy.description: Enter a real wheel diplomacy step and see control markers and hired troops resolve together.

steps.overview: Diplomacy decides regional relationships, not just marker flipping; hiring decides where new troops can actually appear.
steps.wheelEntry: Push the wheel into Diplomacy / Hire first. This action is about map relationship and stationing space, not battle.
steps.chooseTarget: Now read which friendly region is projecting influence outward before deciding how the neighboring control marker changes.
steps.friendlyMark: A friendly marker creates a region you may pass through and station in. Only after that can it be pushed further into tribute or control.
steps.tributeMark: Once it turns into tribute, it becomes a true controlled region. Tribute and friendly areas do not behave the same way.
steps.removeMark: Diplomacy is not only about placing your own marker. It can also roll back someone else's presence.
steps.hireOnly: After the relationship is set, resolve the hired troops. Hiring puts fresh force directly into your controlled area.
steps.finish: Diplomacy changes who the region answers to; hiring changes where force appears. Together they are the real reward of this wheel action.

yearAndCharacters.title: Midyear, Characters, And Chronology
yearAndCharacters.description: See Midyear checks, New Year maintenance, chronology scoring, and how a new year reshuffles the game.

steps.overview: When the shared wheel reaches Midyear and New Year, the whole year catches up at once. Seven Hatreds is not only about the move in front of you.
steps.advanceMidyear: Push the wheel into Midyear first. As soon as it crosses, taxes and character checks start resolving immediately.
steps.midyearTax: Read the Midyear summary for taxes first: which controlled regions fed cards back into hand, and which failed to do so.
steps.midyearCharacters: Then read the character and defeat-pressure result. Character checks and defeat markers are where earlier battles come back into the game state.
steps.advanceNewYear: After Midyear, continue into New Year. Crossing into New Year immediately starts maintenance and year-end settlement.
steps.newYearMaintenance: New Year begins with fortification maintenance. Whether you can hold the Great Wall line and frontier fortifications directly shapes the next year's defense.
steps.newYearAttrition: After maintenance comes attrition. Troops that local population cannot support must be paid for or cut back.
steps.chronologyScore: Chronology cards are not just year markers. The leading player must pay cards to take the prestige for that year.
steps.turnOrderRefresh: Once chronology resolves, turn order and available characters refresh together, changing next year's tempo.
steps.finish: A year passing in Seven Hatreds does not only change the date. It reshuffles resources, characters, order, and strategic pressure.

koreaSpecial.title: Korea And Special Map Rules
koreaSpecial.description: Read the map-specific rules around Korea, Hanseong, sea routes, and Shanhaiguan.

steps.overview: Korea, Hanseong, sea routes, and Shanhaiguan are not side notes. They directly change scoring, movement, and defense.
steps.koreaRegion: Read the Korea area first. It has no population, does not supply troops, and does not count for hegemony control, but it does produce Korea cards.
steps.hanseongVp: Hanseong is more than a region. Once Ming loses its starting hold there, whoever controls Hanseong effectively gains 1 prestige.
steps.waterLimit: Sea routes between anchor regions can move at most 2 troops at a time, and troops that use sea movement cannot keep moving over land in the same action.
steps.shanhaiguan: Shanhaiguan is both a city and a special border between Liaoxi and Jizhen. If it stands, the border stays narrow; if it is ruined, that border collapses into plain ground.
steps.finish: These are not optional reminders. They are formal map rules that directly change whether you can defend, break through, or seize key prestige.
